title: AALL 2026 Annual Meeting Preview with Foster and Whytock: Leading with Aloha, Legal AI, and the Future of Law Libraries
author: Jenny Foster · Jessica Whytock

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source provides only conference-registration logistics and an invitation to attend AALL’s Cleveland meeting. It offers no substantive claim about whether legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation or human control.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s main near-term consequence is work and role redesign rather than wholesale professional replacement. It materially extends the cluster by framing redesign for legal information professionals as a question of professional identity and by identifying critical thinking, ethical discernment, contextual judgment, access and equity as the human capabilities that education and professional institutions should strengthen alongside tool fluency.
qs: The critical thinking that we do, the ethical discernment, the human judgment about context and nuance and access and equity that I don’t think algorithms can replicate.

But the next generation of legal information professionals will need to be really fluent in all these tools, yes, but more importantly, then they’ll need to be anchored in our professional identity, our sense of purpose and service.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Moore supports the cluster’s shift from product availability and sticker price to realized operational value. His observations identify concrete mechanisms—poor model selection, context limits, token consumption and usage-based overages—through which inadequate user literacy can reduce performance and increase actual costs. The evidence is observational rather than quantified.
qs: I’ve seen law firm clients whose users just pick the most sophisticated model for everything, toggle on every optional feature available.

So now those users are running into high-cost overages on the frontier models in particular, and they’re realizing that low sticker price per month is not their reality, not when their users  don’t know how to use those tools efficiently and how to control cost.

kp.k: Poor model selection increases latency and exhausts token allowances
kp.d: In the opening discussion, Sam Moore reports recent advisory conversations about frontier models and legal AI platforms. He says many users do not understand model choices and describes law firm users selecting the most sophisticated model and every optional feature, then encountering slow responses and rapidly depleted token limits. This is practitioner observation, not a quantified study.
qs: First is model selection, because a lot of these products give the users a choice of which model they want to use for a given prompt. But most users of these products really have no idea what the difference is.
I’ve seen law firm clients whose users just pick the most sophisticated model for everything, toggle on every optional feature available.
and then are confused as to why responses are taking a long time and why they’re hitting token limits very, very quickly.

kp.k: Large legal documents create context-window management challenges
kp.d: Moore identifies understanding context windows as a practical training need. He reports conversations about crowded chat contexts creating drift and says this matters particularly for legal use cases involving large document uploads. The transcript offers no measured drift rates or comparative model results.
qs: I’ve had several conversations lately about what a context window even is and how it can create drift when it gets crowded in a chat’s context window and why that really matters for legal use cases, which often involve uploading quite large documents, which take up a lot of space in those context windows.

kp.k: Usage-based AI costs challenge legal technology budgeting
kp.d: Moore says law firms and corporate law departments are generally unfamiliar with pay-as-you-go technology pricing, drawing an analogy to historical pay-per-search legal research. He reports high-cost overages, particularly on frontier models, and argues that low advertised monthly prices do not reflect actual expenditure when users lack efficiency and cost-control skills. No expenditure figures are supplied.
qs: Law firms and law departments, I think, are generally not that accustomed to this kind of pay-as-you-go model in technology.
Not unless you’re like me and you recall when the big legal research platforms were on a pay-per-search basis.
So now those users are running into high-cost overages on the frontier models in particular, and they’re realizing that low sticker price per month is not their reality, not when their users
don’t know how to use those tools efficiently and how to control cost.

kp.k: AI heightens the priority of authoritative legal information
kp.d: Jessica Whytock identifies preserving access to authoritative legal information as a priority for her presidency beginning in July 2026. She argues that AI increases its importance by changing how legal sources are accessed, interpreted and used. This is a professional assessment and proposed institutional priority rather than evidence of measured access outcomes.
qs: Doing what we can to preserve access to authoritative legal information feels so important, even more important with AI and how now it changes how we access, how we interpret, how we use legal sources.
So, making sure that we keep that at the forefront of what we’re doing during my term feels really key.

kp.k: Cross-setting collaboration informs AI learning and lawyer preparation
kp.d: Whytock says collaboration among academic, private and government law librarians helps academics understand professional needs and prepare students; she illustrates this with a practitioner panel in her advanced legal research class. Jenny Foster separately describes learning about law firms’ AI use to inform her court setting. These are concrete examples of knowledge exchange, not evidence of improved educational or court outcomes.
qs: I need to know what is happening in other libraries because it informs how we prepare students for their professional lives.
Because of AALL and the people I have met there, I had a panel this year in my advanced legal research class.
But I love hearing what the firms are doing with it and also and and I’m doing reconnaissance for the court so I’m learning about it.

kp.k: AI prompts reconsideration of legal information professionals’ identity
kp.d: Asked about shifts over the next few years, Foster predicts that the central change will be redefining legal information professionals’ distinctive contribution and communicating it to their institutions and communities, rather than simply mastering technology. She reports librarians taking leadership roles across firms, academic innovation labs and courts, while characterising courts as comparatively behind. These are observations and forecasts without systematic supporting data.
qs: I think the biggest shift that we’re gonna see is this fundamental reimagining of what it means to be a legal information professional in our AI-integrated world.
It is really about thinking about that identity question of who we are. What do we uniquely offer, and how do we communicate that to the organizations, communities, and institutions that we serve?

You, Greg, Emily, all the folks in the firm world, all the people in academia who are doing the innovation labs and all those things, and people in the courts too, we are a little behind, but we are still doing the best we can.

kp.k: Human judgment should complement rather than compete with AI
kp.d: Foster recommends building the profession’s response around critical thinking, ethical discernment and contextual human judgment, alongside tool fluency. She expresses the view that algorithms cannot yet replicate these contributions, qualifying this with uncertainty rather than presenting it as an evaluated capability finding. Her proposed professional orientation emphasises purpose and service, not technological competition.
qs: The answer is not to compete with the technology. It is to lean more deeply into the things that we do.

The critical thinking that we do, the ethical discernment, the human judgment about context and nuance and access and equity that I don’t think algorithms can replicate. I mean, they cannot, right? Not yet.

But the next generation of legal information professionals will need to be really fluent in all these tools, yes, but more importantly, then they’ll need to be anchored in our professional identity, our sense of purpose and service.

kp.k: Professional formation requires education, advocacy and leadership pathways
kp.d: Foster proposes that AALL cultivate the foundations for AI-era professional identity over the next several years through education, advocacy, its professional pipeline and member engagement. Whytock’s complementary organisational agenda is to make participation and leadership routes transparent. These are recommendations for sustaining professional development, not findings about AI-driven employment or staffing changes.
qs: Our work over the next several years, we have to cultivate that foundation through educational programming, through advocacy, our pipeline, and the ways Jessica discussed for engaging our members.
I really want to put systems in place that make it very transparent on how you can volunteer for a committee. How do you get chosen to chair a committee?

kp.k: Future preparation requires broader participation and adaptability
kp.d: Whytock explicitly declines certainty about the profession five years ahead. She recommends involving voices beyond traditional colleagues and allies, and remaining flexible and forward-looking as the profession and legal industry change, including in training future lawyers. This is a conditional strategic recommendation, not a specific forecast of tasks or jobs being displaced.
qs: In a time of tremendous flux, it is hard to know what things will look like in five years.
I do think one of the things that we need to do is make sure that we’re inviting the right people and voices in the room and that we don’t always just lean on our traditional colleagues and allies

As we watch our profession and the legal industry change, it is going to be important to be flexible, adaptable, welcoming, and forward-thinking about who we need to talk to so that we are doing the work that we need to do and that we are teaching and training future lawyers to do the work that they need.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sam Moore says inadequate understanding of model selection and usage-based pricing is creating delays, token-limit problems and unexpected costs for legal AI users.
pts.d: In the opening advisory segment (00:11–02:35), Moore reports that users often do not understand the models offered by frontier-model products and legal AI platforms. Selecting the most sophisticated model and enabling every optional feature can mean slow responses and rapidly exhausted token allowances. He also says law firms and law departments are generally unfamiliar with this technology pricing model, and that inefficient use produces overages, particularly on frontier models, making advertised monthly prices misleading as a guide to actual expenditure.

pts.k: Moore says crowded context windows can produce drift, with particular relevance to document-heavy legal use cases.
pts.d: Moore identifies understanding context windows as a practical requirement for legal AI use. His account connects uploading large legal documents with consumption of context-window capacity and the risk of drift. He does not define drift, quantify its frequency or report a measured effect on legal accuracy.

pts.k: Jessica Whytock says AI is already changing access to, interpretation of and use of legal sources, increasing the importance of preserving authoritative legal information.
pts.d: At 28:03–31:16, Whytock frames preservation of access to authoritative legal information as an especially important professional responsibility in an AI-mediated information environment. This is a qualitative assessment of law librarianship's importance, not a quantified claim about research performance or access-to-justice outcomes.

pts.k: Jenny Foster predicts that AI integration will fundamentally redefine legal information professionals' identity and distinctive contribution, rather than merely require learning new technology.
pts.d: In her future-facing answer at 34:48–37:19, Foster says librarians should deepen their critical thinking, ethical discernment and contextual human judgment rather than compete with technology. She expects the next generation to combine tool fluency with a strong professional identity and service orientation. She also reports that librarians are already taking leadership roles in firms, academic innovation settings and courts, while characterising courts as somewhat behind. Her account emphasises adaptation and complementary human capabilities rather than predicting job elimination.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Moore relies on recent advisory conversations and observed client behaviour; Foster and Whytock offer professional observations and judgments, not formal empirical results.
pts.d: Moore explicitly grounds his operational claims in Legal Technology Hub advisory work and personal encounters with law firm clients. He supplies no usage logs, cost figures, model comparisons or benchmarks. Foster points to members' work in firms, academia and courts as evidence of emerging leadership roles, but her prediction about professional identity and her assessment of human capabilities are expressed as beliefs. Whytock offers her professional assessment of AI's effect on legal information without citing a study or specific case. The transcript supplies no quantitative evidence for these claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Operational problems and changes in legal-source use are described as current in 2026; Foster's professional transformation is unfolding now and over the next several years.
pts.d: Moore refers to the preceding week or two of advisory conversations and says the token-usage issue predates the launch of Claude for legal, although that launch appears to have stimulated discussion. His cost claims are conditional on inefficient use and inadequate cost control; context drift is linked to crowded windows. Whytock describes changes in legal-source use as happening now and makes preservation a priority for her forthcoming presidency. Foster's forecast concerns an AI-integrated world and the next generation of professionals, with an educational and advocacy response over several years. She qualifies her statement that algorithms cannot replicate the identified human capabilities with 'Not yet.' Whytock's closing response explicitly declines confidence about the five-year outlook rather than making a definite AI forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are legal AI users and technology buyers, law librarians across institutional settings, and the people and organisations relying on legal information.
pts.d: Moore identifies law firms and corporate law departments as facing unfamiliar variable technology costs, and their users as needing better model-selection, context-window and token-management knowledge. Foster's forecast covers legal information professionals in private firms, academic institutions and courts, especially emerging professionals who will need both AI fluency and distinctive human judgment. AALL is assigned a supporting role through education, advocacy and professional development. Whytock emphasises law librarians' responsibility to sustain access to authoritative sources. Organisations, communities and institutions served by librarians are the intended beneficiaries; no client savings, staffing reductions or measured public-access gains are specified.
